title: Friends you never met
translation: Nothing beats sitting alone by the lamp with a book open, making friends with people who lived centuries before you. As for books: the moving parts of the Wen Xuan, Bai Juyi's poems, Laozi, Zhuangzi. And our own scholars, the old ones at least, wrote plenty that's moving too.
original: ひとり{灯火|ともしび}のもとに{文|ふみ}をひろげて、{見|み}ぬ{世|よ}の{人|ひと}を{友|とも}とするこそ、こよなう{慰|なぐさ}むわざなれ。
{文|ふみ}は{文選|もんぜん}のあはれなる{巻々|まきまき}、{白氏文集|はくしもんじふ}、{老子|らうじ}のことば、{南華|なんくわ}の{篇|へん}。
この{国|くに}の{博士|はかせ}どもの{書|か}けるものも、いにしへのは、あはれなる{事|こと}{多|おほ}かり。
literal: Alone under the lamp, spreading out a book and making friends with people of a world one never saw: that is an incomparably comforting thing.
As for books: the moving volumes of the Wen Xuan, the collected works of Bai Juyi, the words of Laozi, the chapters of Nanhua (Zhuangzi).
What the scholars of this country wrote, too, the old ones, has many moving things.

notes.quote: 見ぬ世の人を友とする
notes.text: 'To make friends with people of a world you never saw': one of the most quoted lines in the book. こそ … なれ closes it.
The Wen Xuan, a sixth-century Chinese anthology of poetry and prose. Every educated Japanese reader knew it.
The collected works of Bai Juyi (772–846), the Chinese poet who was most loved in Japan. The Tale of Genji quotes him constantly, and the Pillow Book often.

notes.quote: 老子のことば、南華の篇
notes.text: Laozi and Zhuangzi ('Nanhua' is a title of the Zhuangzi), the classics of Daoism. The 1925 edition reads 老子 as らうじ; the usual reading is らうし.
Japanese scholars who wrote in Chinese. Even here he prefers the old ones.
